clinicalPearls: Enterobiasis is caused by the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis and is the commonest helminth infection in temperate regions, particularly among school-age children
The cardinal symptom is nocturnal perianal and perineal itching, caused by the gravid female migrating to the anus at night to deposit eggs on the perianal skin
Transmission is faecal-oral via ingestion of eggs, readily spread within households and institutions by contaminated hands, bedding and fomites, and autoinfection sustains the cycle
Eggs are not usually found in stool; the perianal cellulose tape (sticky tape) test applied in the early morning is the diagnostic method of choice
The eggs are characteristically oval and flattened on one side, and adult worms may occasionally be seen at the anus
In girls, aberrant migration can rarely cause vulvovaginitis or involvement of the genital tract
Treatment with pyrantel, albendazole or mebendazole is given with a repeat dose after about two weeks and treatment of household contacts, alongside hygiene measures
reference.pathophysiology: Enterobius vermicularis is a small white nematode whose adults inhabit the caecum and adjacent colon. At night the gravid female migrates through the anus and deposits large numbers of sticky eggs on the perianal skin, which become infective within hours. Scratching in response to the intense pruritus contaminates the fingers, and eggs are then transferred to the mouth, to others, or onto bedding and surfaces; ingested eggs hatch and mature in the intestine. This ready autoinfection and person-to-person transmission explain the tendency to recur and to affect whole households. The disease is generally benign, with pruritus reflecting the local irritant and inflammatory response to egg deposition rather than tissue invasion.
additionalDifferentials: Candidal or other perianal skin infection
additionalInvestigations: Perianal cellulose tape test in the early morning for eggs
Repeated tape testing on consecutive mornings to improve yield
Direct inspection of the perianal region for adult worms
Microscopy of subungual scrapings in selected cases
Stool microscopy, recognising it has low sensitivity for this infection
Assessment of household contacts when recurrence occurs
redFlags: Persistent recurrence despite treatment suggesting ongoing reinfection within the household
Genitourinary or pelvic symptoms from aberrant worm migration
Secondary bacterial infection of excoriated perianal skin
Marked sleep disturbance and distress in a child
reference.prognosis: Excellent; infection is benign and readily cured, though reinfection is common and eradication depends on treating close contacts and maintaining hygiene.
pitfalls: Relying on stool microscopy, which usually misses the diagnosis, instead of the tape test
Treating the index case alone and omitting household contacts
Failing to give the recommended repeat dose, allowing relapse from autoinfection
Overlooking pinworm as a cause of paediatric vulvovaginitis
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Give first-line antihelminthic treatment with a benzimidazole such as mebendazole or albendazole, or pyrantel pamoate as an alternative
Repeat the anthelmintic dose after an interval to eliminate worms maturing from surviving eggs
Treat the whole household and close contacts simultaneously to interrupt autoinfection and reinfection
Reinforce hygiene measures including handwashing, keeping nails short, discouraging scratching, and morning washing of the perianal area
Launder bedding, nightclothes and towels and clean surfaces to remove environmental eggs
Manage recurrence by re-treating contacts and reinforcing hygiene rather than assuming drug failure
Use antihelminthics with caution in pregnancy, weighing timing and severity of infection
